```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
required <- c("dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "sf", "readr", "scales", "jsonlite", "knitr")
missing <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) stop("Install missing packages: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
invisible(lapply(required, library, character.only = TRUE))
options(timeout = max(180, getOption("timeout")))
post_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE), mustWork = TRUE))
raw_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "data", "raw")
results_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "results")
fig_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "figures")
for (p in c(raw_dir, results_dir, fig_dir)) dir.create(p, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
source(file.path(post_dir, "scripts", "data.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
source(file.path(post_dir, "scripts", "analysis.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
state_borders <- shapes |> group_by(STATEFP) |> summarise(.groups = "drop")
```

A factory town and a county with many business-service jobs may both be highly specialized, yet offer different opportunities to residents. **Where are manufacturing and professional/business services concentrated, how did their jobs change from 2019 to 2024, and does specialization coincide with higher household income?** These questions matter when communities consider whether attracting a particular industry will improve local living standards.

I combine BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) annual employment with Census county boundaries and ACS household income. The maps cover the contiguous 48 states and Washington, DC; Alaska, Hawaii, and territories are outside the displayed study area. Employment counts jobs at workplaces, whereas ACS describes residents. Professional/business services is a broad sector that includes management, administrative support, and waste services as well as professional and technical work; it is not a pure measure of high-skill jobs.

## Where does each sector matter most locally?

County size makes job counts difficult to compare. Instead, a **location quotient** measures a sector's local private-employment share relative to its published U.S. share:

$$
LQ_{ic}=\frac{E_{ic}/E_c}{E_{i,US}/E_{US}}.
$$

An LQ of 2 means twice the national employment share, not twice the number of jobs, productivity, or wages. Both numerators and denominators use private ownership. The U.S. benchmark comes directly from national QCEW records, rather than summing incomplete county reports.

```{r}
#| label: fig-specialization
#| fig-cap: "Private-sector employment concentration, 2024. Both panels use identical LQ classes; gray is unavailable, not zero. U.S. national benchmarks include all U.S. counties, while maps display the contiguous states and DC. Sources: BLS QCEW and Census 2024 cartographic boundaries; author calculations."
#| fig-alt: "Two county maps comparing manufacturing and professional/business-service location quotients, with a shared legend and state outlines."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
map_data <- shapes |> left_join(current, by = "GEOID")
p <- ggplot(map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = lq_band), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = state_borders, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = .18, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c("#eff3ff", "#bdd7e7", "#4292c6", "#084594", "#bdbdbd"), lq_levels),
                    drop = FALSE, name = "Location quotient") +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(5070), datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Concentration is about local importance, not county size") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
                                    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15))
save_figure(p, "figure1_specialization_maps.png", height = 9)
```

Manufacturing specialization forms a broad belt across the Midwest and Southeast; business-service specialization is more scattered. Among counties with LQ at least 1.5, the three largest manufacturing employment bases are **`r example_text('Manufacturing')`**; for professional/business services they are **`r example_text('Professional/business services')`**. Selecting examples by employment avoids mistaking a tiny county's extreme LQ for a large job center. Map area represents land, not workers. Dark counties indicate local reliance on a sector, relevant when investigating exposure to industry-wide shocks; they do not by themselves measure vulnerability or resilience.

## Concentration and growth answer different questions

A sector can remain prominent locally while losing jobs. Figure 2 therefore compares **annual-average employment in 2019 and 2024**, using the same percentage-change classes for both sectors. These endpoints describe net change across the pandemic period, not the timing or cause of that change.

```{r}
#| label: fig-growth
#| fig-cap: "Private-sector job change, 2019–2024. Gray includes suppressed/missing endpoints, fewer than 100 sector jobs in 2019, and Connecticut's changed county boundaries. Classes have open-ended tails; values are not clipped. Sources: BLS QCEW and Census boundaries."
#| fig-alt: "Two county maps show where each sector's employment grew or declined between 2019 and 2024. Excluded counties are gray."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
growth_map <- shapes |> left_join(growth, by = "GEOID")
growth_levels <- levels(growth$change_band)
p <- ggplot(growth_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = change_band), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = state_borders, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = .18, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c("#b2182b", "#ef8a62", "#f7f7f7", "#67a9cf", "#2166ac", "#bdbdbd"),
                                     growth_levels), drop = FALSE, name = "Job change",
                    guide = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(5070), datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Established concentrations did not all follow the same path") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
                                    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15))
save_figure(p, "figure2_employment_change_maps.png", height = 9)
```

Manufacturing employment grew in **`r percent(sector_stat(growth_summary, 'Manufacturing', 'share_gained'))`** of `r sector_stat(growth_summary, 'Manufacturing', 'n_counties')` comparable counties, versus **`r percent(sector_stat(growth_summary, 'Professional/business services', 'share_gained'))`** of `r sector_stat(growth_summary, 'Professional/business services', 'n_counties')` for business services. These are shares of counties, not shares of workers. Their matched-sample employment totals changed by `r percent(sector_stat(growth_summary, 'Manufacturing', 'matched_job_change'))` and `r percent(sector_stat(growth_summary, 'Professional/business services', 'matched_job_change'))`, respectively. Different sample sizes mean these are not national growth estimates.

Suppressed observations are never treated as zero. The 100-job starting threshold limits unstable percentage changes in tiny employment bases. Connecticut appears in the 2024 concentration map but is excluded from growth: its new planning regions do not map directly to the old counties. The saved coverage audit reports every exclusion.

## Does specialization coincide with higher resident income?

```{r}
#| label: fig-income
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of county median household income by 2024 sector concentration. Income is the ACS 2020–2024 five-year estimate, expressed in 2024 dollars. Each county has equal weight; boxes show the median and interquartile range, whiskers extend to 1.5 IQR, and points are outliers. This is not the distribution of individual household incomes. Sources: Census ACS and BLS QCEW."
#| fig-alt: "Two boxplot panels compare county median household incomes below versus at or above the national sector employment share. Each group shows its county count."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
p <- ggplot(income_sample, aes(concentration, income, fill = concentration)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .55, outlier.size = .6, outlier.alpha = .25) +
  geom_text(data = income_summary, aes(x = concentration, y = 0, label = paste0("n = ", n_counties)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#bdd7e7", "#4292c6"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Below U.S.\nshare", "At/above U.S.\nshare")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = .001, suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(.03, .06))) +
  labs(title = "Specialization does not identify a county's living standard",
        x = NULL, y = "County median household income (2024 dollars)") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
save_figure(p, "figure3_income_comparison.png", height = 5.5)
```

The median county income among counties at or above the national manufacturing share is **`r gap_text(income_gap('Manufacturing'))`** than among counties below it. The corresponding business-services difference is **`r gap_text(income_gap('Professional/business services'))`**. Counties within each group still span a wide income range. Excluding income estimates whose 90% margin of error exceeds 30% of the estimate changes those differences to `r gap_text(income_gap('Manufacturing', income_sensitivity))` and `r gap_text(income_gap('Professional/business services', income_sensitivity))`; this precision screen is a sensitivity check, not a significance test.

Income summarizes **2020–2024**, not a single-year 2024 observation. Commuting, household composition, education, and local living costs can all affect the comparison. Income is not adjusted for geographic price differences, and these unadjusted group comparisons cannot show that specialization caused higher or lower incomes, population movement, or skills accumulation.

## Takeaway

Industrial geography tells us where a sector matters locally; employment change tells us whether its job base expanded; resident income asks who may share in local prosperity. None substitutes for the others. Communities can use the maps to identify places for closer investigation, but choosing an industry-development strategy also requires evidence about job access, commuting, wages, and costs that this descriptive analysis does not establish.

## Sources and replication

[BLS QCEW annual CSV slices](https://www.bls.gov/cew/additional-resources/open-data/csv-data-slices.htm), [industry definitions](https://www.bls.gov/cew/classifications/industry/industry-titles.htm), [Connecticut's 2024 geography break](https://www.bls.gov/cew/classifications/areas/new-2024-connecticut-counties.htm), [2024 ACS five-year income table B19013](https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/groups/B19013.html), and [Census cartographic boundaries](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/cartographic-boundary.html).

All downloads, source URLs, checksums, derived tables, validation results, and figures are saved locally. Existing snapshots are reused without network requests or API credentials. [Replication instructions and limitations](README.md) document the sample, missing data, thresholds, coordinate system, dependencies, and refresh procedure. The complete acquisition and analysis scripts are linked in that README.
